# Correctness isn't Everything

## Let's Go Shopping (version 1) 

:::::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

```python
define shopping_trip1(grocery_list: List[food_item])
                      -> pantry_list: List[food_item]:

  # List of food in the pantry so far.
  pantry_list = []

  for item_on_grocery_list in grocery_list:
    # Take paper with single item to the store.
    item_at_store = go_to_store(item_on_grocery_list)
    # Get the item from the shelf.
    item_in_cart = pick_at_store(item_at_store)
    # Bring the item home.
    item_at_home = return_from_store(item_in_cart)
    # Put the item away.
    pantry_list.append(put_in_pantry(item_at_home))

  return pantry_list
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```scheme
(define shopping-trip1 grocery-list
  (cond [(empty? grocery-list) '()],
        [else
          (cons (put-in-pantry
                  (return-from-store
                    (pick-at-store
                      (go-to-store (first grocery-list)))))
                (shopping-trip1 (rest grocery-list)))]))
```

::: {.div style="margin-top: 150px; font-size: large"}

I am being sloppy here by assuming that the helper functions can accept (and will return) either a single item or a list of items

:::

:::

::::::


If we have $n$ items in our list, how long does this procedure take?

::: notes

* How long to `go_to_store`?
* How long to `pick_at_store`?
* How long to `return_from_store`?
* How long to `put_in_pantry`?

:::


## Let's Go Shopping (version 2)

:::::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

```python
define shopping_trip2(grocery_list: List[food_item])
                      -> pantry_list: List[food_item]:

  # Take piece of paper with list to the store.
  grocery_list_at_store = go_to_store(grocery_list)

  # Get all items on the list into the cart.
  cart_list = []
  for item_at_store in grocery_list_at_store:
    cart_list.append(pick_at_store(item_at_store))

  # Bring the items home.
  grocery_bags_at_home = return_from_store(cart_list)

  # Put the items away.
  pantry_list = []
  for item_at_home in grocery_bags_at_home:
    pantry_list.append(put_in_pantry(item_at_home))

  return pantry_list
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```scheme
(define shopping-trip2 grocery-list
  (let ([grocery-list-at-store (go-to-store grocery-list)])
    (put-in-pantry
      (return-from-store
        (pick-at-store grocery-list-at-store)))))
```

::: {.div style="margin-top: 200px; font-size: large"}

I am being sloppy here by assuming that the helper functions can accept (and will return) either a single item or a list of items

:::

:::

::::::


If we have $n$ items in our list, how long does this procedure take?

::: notes

* Go to the store just once.
* Return from the store just once.

* As $n$ gets larger, total time will increasingly be determined by those parts of the procedure which depend on $n$.
* For large $n$, we can essentially ignore the stuff which grows more slowly (or not at all) with $n$.

:::

## Quantifying the task... {.medium}

If we are solving a problem / writing an algorithm for an input of arbitrary size, we can parameterize the running time of the solution by the size of the input.

We usually denote this input size using the variable $n$.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="25%"}

![](/images/pixelated-chevron-knitting-pattern.jpg){fig-alt="A pixelated knitting pattern."}

:::

::: {.column width="75%"}

- We need to specify what $n$ represents (in this case the length of each side of the square).
- Sometimes we need multiple parameters to describe the size of the problem (such as $n$ and $m$).
- We pay attention to only the degree of n (so if a scarf takes $3n^2 + 12n$ time, we are only interested in the fact it is $n^2$)

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
* In this example we choose to label $n$ as the side-length in stitches, but other choices are possible.
* We don't care so much about units, so we communicate using the largest order term
  * A scarf which is always $3n \cross n$ takes time $3n^2$ to knit, we ignore the 3 when we're talking about algorithms. It's the squared part that really determines how waiting time increases as the problem size increases.
  * We say that the variable term "dominates".

But why did we introduce a "parameter"? What happened to the rows and stitches? What does this have to do with a computer processing data? 

We are seeking to understand the effort / efficiency / complexity of solving the problem / running the algorithm in a simple / elegant manner, where we have abstracted away the clutter of the details of the problem.
:::


##  {.center background-image="/images/steve-jobs.jpg" background-opacity="0.3" background-size="contain" background-position="bottom right" data-menu-title="Steve Jobs quote" font-size="medium"}

> Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
> It takes a lot of hard work to make something simple, to truly understand the underlying challenges and come up with **elegant** solutions.
> \[...\] It's not just minimalism or the absence of clutter.
> It involves digging through the depth of complexity.
> To be truly simple, you have to go really deep.
> \[...\] You have to understand the essence of a product in order to be able to get rid of the parts that are not essential.
>
> --- **Steve Jobs**



::: notes

In this course we will be seeking simplicity and elegance not only in our algorithms, but also in how we analyze them.  In particular, when looking at the complexity of an algorithm we will ignore the constants and dominated terms. 

Our software should be considered to be a means of communicating with other humans who want to know how we have solved the problem. Humans are not good readers, but they think they are good programmers, so if they cannot understand our solution, then they will just rewrite it! (Complexity gives people a reason not to connect)

# Analyzing Complexity

## Handcraft and Code {.smaller}

**Knitting model:**

::::: columns
::: {.column }

- Side length is $n$

- One stitch is a unit of work

:::
::: {.column }

- $n$ rows, $n$ stitches per row

- Total work is $n^2$

:::
:::::

```{pyodide}
def knit_square_count(n):
    cloth = ""
    for row in range(n):          # n rows
        for col in range(n):      # n stitches per row
            cloth += "X"          # unit work
        cloth += "\n"             # go to next row
    return cloth

print(knit_square_count(5))
```

::: notes
Walk through code.  Yes, we are mutating variable `cloth`, and we generally discourage mutation.  Are we mutating the string to which `cloth` refers?

Count work to arrive at $n^2$ conclusion.
* Which line is executed most frequently? 
* How many times is outer `for` loop executed?
* How many total times is line 5 (inner `for` loop) executed?
:::


## Quantifying the task...

Suppose we can knit 1 (= 10^0^) stitches per second….

The degree (in n) makes a very big difference!

| time \\ n | 10 | 100 | 1000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| log n | ~3 s | ~6½ s | ~10 s |
| n | 10 s | 10^2^ s ~ 1½ min | 10^3^ s ~ 16½ min |
| n log n | 3(10) s ~ ½ min | 6(10^2^) s ~ 10 min | 10^4^ s ~ 2½ hours |
| n^2^ | 100 s ~ 1½ min | 10^4^ s ~ 2½ hours | 10^6^ s ~ 11½ days |
| n^3^ | 1000 s ~ 16½ min | 10^6^ s ~ 11½ days | 10^9^ s ~ 31½ years |
| 2^n^ | 1024 s ~ 17 min | ~10^30^ s | ~10^301^ s |

Notes: "log" = log_2 and the age of the universe: ~10^18 s

::: {.notes}
Log factors are great!
Linear (power 1) is good.
Powers 2+ (polynomial) is okay as long as n is reasonably small.
If n is in the exponent, forget about it…
:::



## Quantifying the task...

But computers are much faster. Suppose we can "knit" 10^12^ stitches / s

The amount of computation we do inside our algorithm actually matters!

| time \\ n | 10 | 100 | 1000 | 10^6^ | 10^12^ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| log n | ~3(10^-12^) s | ~6½(10^-12^) s | ~10(10^-12^) s | ~20(10^-12^) s | ~40(10^-12^) s |
| n | 10^-11^ s | 10^-10^ s | 10^-9^ s | 10^-6^ s | 1 s |
| n log n | 3(10^-11^) s | 6(10^-10^) s | 10^-8^ s | ~20(10^-6^) s | ~40 s |
| n^2^ | 10^-10^ s | 10^-8^ s | 10^-6^ s | 1 s | 10^12^ s |
| n^3^ | 10^-9^ s | 10^-6^ s | 10^-3^ s | 10^6^ s | 10^24^ s |
| 2^n^ | ~10^-9^ s | ~10^18^ s | ~10^289^ s |  |  |

Notes: proteins fold in ~10^-6^ s and the age of the universe: ~10^18^ s

::: {.notes}
A fast laptop might achieve 10^12 flops. Fastest supercomputer is 2198 x 10^15 flops.

If our rag/data size is 1000, and we need to compute $n^3$ steps/stitches (like knitting a cube!!), then the total time is 1000^3/10^12 == 10^-3 or one thousandth of a second. Nbd.

BUT let's look at bigger data. 10^12 (~128gb … pretty big) 10^12 mm == 10^6 km (for reference, 384,400 km to the moon or 149(10^6) km to the sun.  Knitting something that big would take 10^12 seconds ~32000 years. The sun will long since have burnt out by 10^18

Punchline -- we don't want to do $2^n$ amount of computation, and we need creative approaches for big data.

Recap -- we've seen a problem whose size we characterize by $n^2$, we'll see problems whose time we characterize by $n$, for sure, and later in the term, we'll see a problem which is very simply stated, whose size we characterize by $2^n$. :(
:::
